title: The changing landscape and challenges of shark conservation and management, 1980s to present

authors.affiliation: Save our Seas Foundation

abstract_text: Prior to the 1980s, suggestions that the conservation and management of sharks, skates and rays warranted attention were more likely to raise quizzical eyebrows than to generate action in governmental and non-governmental marine policy circles. This presentation will review how and why this picture has changed over the decades. It will cover increased public awareness and shark research; trends in demand for elasmobranch products and ecotourism services; the struggle to promote and adopt fisheries management measures; the rise of the shark conservation NGOs, and the recent inclusion of commercially-important species in the Appendices of major biodiversity environment instruments (the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species–CITES, and the Conservation of Migratory Species–CMS). While there are many achievements to celebrate, the future of shark conservation now stands upon the cusp: failure to implement Shark Plans and to deliver sustainable trade management under CITES threatens not only the survival of many shark populations, but possibly also the continued engagement and support of governments, biodiversity conventions and even the public.

title: The role of the elasmobranchs in the Italian implementation of the EU Marine Strategy Framework Directive (MSFD)

authors.affiliation: Italian National Institute for Environmental Protection and Research (ISPRA)

abstract_text: The European Union Marine Strategy Framework Directive (MSFD) has the objective of achieving or maintaining Good Environmental Status (GES) in European seas by 2020. The first requirement was the “initial assessment” of the status of marine waters in relation to eleven qualitative “descriptors of GES”. In particular, the “descriptor 1” requires that “the biological diversity is maintained” and it includes elasmobranchs. In order to pursue this goal, Italy decided to analyse all the available information on the elasmobranchs in the National waters and specific attention was devoted to the analysis of data of the EU MEDITS project (International Bottom Trawl Survey in the Mediterranean), for the period 1994-2011. Based on this information the “initial assessment” was performed. Moreover the functional group of the “demersal elasmobranchs” was proposed for two indicators to evaluate the GES: “condition of the typical species and communities” and the "relative abundance and/or biomass", and the associated metrics (the Shannon-Wiener diversity index and the abundance and biomass of piscivorous species). The contribution of these two indicators to the GES is based on temporal trend analyses. For these two indicators was proposed an operational target directly linked to management actions related to initiatives devoted to inform and increase awareness of professional fishermen on the best practices of handling and release of by-catches. The next key steps are the start-up of these activities that should be conceived in line with similar initiative defined by other EU Member States.

title: Chondrichthyan fish of the British Isles: prioritising species for further study and the utility of Ecological Risk Assessments for informing management

authors.affiliation: Centre for Environment, Fisheries and Aquaculture Science (CEFAS), UK

abstract_text: An updated taxonomic list of chondrichthyans reported from around the British Isles was compiled, with 80 species from the area. A prioritisation exercise was performed for all these species, with species scored qualitatively under four categories (conservation interest; commercial importance; biological vulnerability; and importance of the UK to the species range). Those species that ranked highest were subsequently investigated in terms of data availability and data gaps, and whether or not ICES has been able to evaluate the stock status and formulate advice. This exercise can serve as an evidence base to better identify those data collection programmes (biological sampling and/or field studies) that could usefully be undertaken to inform appropriate regional management. Alternative approaches for prioritising species of interest, acting at a finer fishery-based scale, are Productivity Susceptibility Analyses (PSA). A PSA of the Celtic Seas skate complex interaction with demersal gillnet and trawl fleets was trialled at ICES this year. The preliminary results, suggested refinements and future direction of such methods are discussed in relation to management of data limited elasmobranch fisheries.

title: Who Ray?! DNA barcoding unveils skate species diversity in ‘ray’ products sold across Ireland and the UK

authors.affiliation: University of Salford, UK

abstract_text: Recent food mislabelling scandals have ensured that food authenticity has a very high profile, with molecular methods to identify species in foods gaining renewed interest. Applications of DNA barcoding for identifying elasmobranch species have been very successful during investigations of the damaging trade in shark fins, helping inform management and conservation decisions. But whilst considerable effort has been spent identifying the species sold in shark products, little attention has focused on sales of skate (Rajidae). Skates are widely consumed across the globe, but many large species are subject to considerable concern for their conservation, with limits placed on the landings. Yet within the EU, sale of skates is still made under a blanket term of ‘ray’ with the fish only valued for their wings. So before sale, their bodies are usually discarded and often skinned, making morphological identification impossible. For the first time, DNA barcoding was applied to samples of skate wings traded across the British Isles. The results showed that five species were commonly being sold (Raja brachyura, Raja montagui, Raja clavata, Leucoraja naevus & Raja microocellata) and indicated that endangered species are not being passed on to consumers. However, the investigation highlights that the sale of skate wings under ambiguous labels makes it extremely difficult for consumers to exercise a right to choose species of less conservation concern. Additionally, in the minority of cases where ray wings were labelled with species names a high level of mislabelling was identified.

title: DNA barcoding of the Northeast Atlantic skates (Chondrichthyes: Rajidae), with remarks on the widely distributed Starry Ray Amblyraja radiata

authors.affiliation: UiT The Arctic University of Norway

abstract_text: Morphological identification of skates is difficult for non-specialists due to morphological conservatism between species and high intraspecific variation due to factors such as ontogenetic changes. Being an understudied group, changes in taxonomy are still made and species boundaries are debated. Here, we analysed the mitochondrial ‘barcode gene’, COI, from a total of 175 specimens distributed in 15 species and 6 genera in the North Atlantic Ocean. A barcode gap was confirmed between all species pairs, facilitating unambiguous genetic identification of species. This is the first study that uses COI to successfully separate the cryptic Dipturus batis, and the first genetic evidence on the reallocation of Dipturus linteus to Rajella lintea. This is also the first report of Raja montagui from Norwegian waters. A remarkably high number of haplotypes was found in the Starry Ray Amblyraja radiata. Due to striking differences in life history parameters, particularly size at maturity, cryptic species diversity has previously been suspected in this group. There was, however, no concordance between haplotype and morphotype and the present data do not support any subdivision of the Starry Ray.

title: The skate complex of the British Isles: current status, discard survival and management options

authors.affiliation: Centre for Environment, Fisheries and Aquaculture Science (CEFAS), UK

abstract_text: The composition and abundance of the skate assemblage around the British Isles has changed over the last century. The largest species (e.g. White Skate Rostroraja alba) are near extirpated from former habitats, whilst the populations of smaller-bodied species (e.g. Spotted Ray Raja montagui and Thornback Ray R. clavata) appear healthier. Current management regulations for skates include quota for the complex as a whole, prohibited status for some of the more vulnerable species and, in some inshore waters of England and Wales, a minimum landing size. The efficacy of these and other potential measures is highly dependent on whether fish survive discarding. Here we provide a synthesis of skate fisheries around the British Isles, the discard and retention patterns of skates in various fisheries and available information on skate survivorship. Short-term survival for longline-caught skates was high, although overnight soak times increased jaw damage. Skates taken in inshore gillnet fisheries also had a high survival, ranging from 98% (<24 hour soak time) to about 88% (43–48 hour soak time). In contrast, the survivorship of skates captured by beam trawl was lower, with about half the fish surviving. Improving our knowledge of the survivorship of skates taken in various fisheries not only helps inform on assessment and management of the stocks, but will also provide relevant information in relation to proposed discard bans under the reformed Common Fisheries Policy.

title: How many gulper shark species are there? Revisiting the North Atlantic species diversity of a troubled deepwater shark group - the genus Centrophorus

authors.affiliation: CIBIO – Center for Research in Biodiversity and Genetic Resources, Portugal

abstract_text: The gulper sharks are a group of medium-sized benthopelagic sharks usually found on continental and insular slopes of the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific oceans. Many of the 13-15 recognized species are routinely caught in mid- and deep-water fisheries worldwide and some have shown a considerable decline in abundance in the last few decades. Despite the need for efficient and sustainable management of these species, clear and consistent species discrimination and taxonomic identification of Centrophorus remains problematic. We used molecular (COI and 16S gene sequences) and morphometric data to re-evaluate the diversity of Centrophorus in the North Atlantic, including the Gulf of Mexico and the Mediterranean Sea. Data were collected from fresh specimens caught by commercial and research vessels, from preserved specimens deposited in museum and research institute collections, and from publicly available databases (e.g. GenBank). Molecular data separated North Atlantic Centrophorus specimens into five well-supported groups while morphometric measurements corroborated the existence of these five groups but indicated the presence of three additional groups for which no molecular data were available. Comparison of North Atlantic specimens with those collected elsewhere showed that four of the five groups identified above also occur in the Indian and/or Pacific oceans. Our results extend the reported range of some species considerably and suggest that most Centrophorus have wider geographic distributions than previously reported.

title: Biological studies to inform management of Smoothhounds Mustelus spp. in the Northeast Atlantic

authors.affiliation: Centre for Environment, Fisheries and Aquaculture Science (CEFAS), UK

abstract_text: Seasonal catches of Starry Smoothhound Mustelus asterias have been commonplace around the UK coast for many years. However, until recently, all but the largest of these have predominantly been discarded due to a low commercial value. In the 33 year time-series of national landings reported to ICES, Smoothhound catches are at an all-time high, with nearly 3,000 t reported in 2012. Within parts of the UK, Smoothhound landings have increased in recent years, which may relate to increased abundance in northern European waters and/or emerging market opportunities. In terms of the latter, anecdotal accounts from the fishing industry suggest that this is in part a response to the current zero catch of Spurdog Squalus acanthias. Following a prioritisation exercise of the chondrichthyans of the British Isles, this species was deemed to be a high priority for study, given its life history, importance of UK waters to the stock and the emerging commercial interest. As little is known regarding many aspects of the biology of this species, a biological sampling programme was initiated to help collect life history parameters necessary for future stock assessments and management measures to be appraised. Monthly samples of Mustelus have been obtained since June, and fully dissected. Preliminary data on conversion factors, maturity and fecundity information and hepatosomatic indices are presented, with comments made on the utility of these for informing on future management.

title: Sharks within the MSFD – from national to international

authors.affiliation: Nederlandse Elasmobranchen Vereniging / Dutch Elasmobranch Society

abstract_text: Following the recommendations made in the Dutch Shark Action Plan, the Dutch government will address the management and conservation of sharks and skates through the implementation of the Marine Framework Strategy. The mainstay will be Descriptor 1 with the objective to retain biodiversity. The Dutch Elasmobranch Society (NEV) has been asked to advise the government on a management plan by 2014. The primary aim of the plan will be to improve the size, distribution and condition of the populations of sharks and rays on the Dutch continental shelf and will be part of the Dutch management plan to be presented to the European Commission. The project has three phases: (1) to identify the current and historical status of the elasmobranchs on the Dutch continental shelf (DCS) and to assess the suitability of species to function as indicator species for the whole group; (2) to identify the factors influencing the abundance, distribution and condition of the elasmobranchs on the DCS; and (3) to develop cost-effective management measures. This paper will present the framework and first results of the project. The necessity and possibilities for cooperation and harmonisation at a European level will be discussed.

title: Indicator species selection for elasmobranchs on the Dutch Continental shelf

authors.affiliation: Nederlandse Elasmobranchen Vereniging/Van Hall Larenstein University of Applied Sciences

abstract_text: Indicators provide insight into phenomena and trends that are not directly perceivable. They compress large amounts of information and make it possible to share knowledge in an accessible way. Indicator species are used to determine the state of or change in an ecosystem, habitat or population. The information indicator species provide is for instance needed to monitor the effects of conservation methods. The downside of indicators (species) is that the process of indicator selection is often obscure and unfounded. There is no method available for selection of indicators. Literature on the subject often only describes preparation and not the process of indicator selection itself. The aim of our thesis completed at the ‘NEV’ was to appoint multiple indicator species that indicate the population condition of elasmobranchs on the Dutch Continental Shelf. To do so we developed a method and indicator selection model based on available literature. The model consists of multiple criteria (taking both ecological and legislative factors into account): historical data, monitoring robustness, early warning and international relevance. Each criteria consists of multiple features. How well the elasmobranch species meet the features and criteria will determine how suitable they are as an indicator species. Finally it is possible to express preference for features by assigning different weighting to features that are perceived as important (by for example policy makers or researchers). The model we created makes indicator selection transparent, repeatable and clear. It makes it possible to make an informed decision in regard to indicator selection because the model takes a broad range of factors into account. Finally the model is adaptable (for new knowledge and features) and thus also applicable in other countries.

title: Bycatch and discarding patterns of dogfish and sharks taken in commercial fisheries around the British Isles

authors.affiliation: Centre for Environment, Fisheries and Aquaculture Science (CEFAS), UK

abstract_text: The discard and retention patterns of dogfish and sharks taken as a bycatch in UK commercial fisheries were examined. Data were collected primarily on English vessels fishing on the continental shelf of the North Sea ecoregion (ICES Divisions IV a–c, VIId) and Celtic Seas ecoregion (ICES Divisions VIa, VIIa–c,e–k). Vessels examined represented four main gear types (otter, beam and Nephrops trawls, and gillnet), with only limited data available for longline and mid-water trawl. Beam trawlers generally captured proportionally more small (juvenile) dogfish than otter trawlers. Gillnets were the most size selective gear. Data on the elasmobranch catches from Nephrops trawlers were frequently too limited to draw an accurate discard/retention pattern, which may reflect a low catchability of sharks by this gear and/or that elasmobranchs are not abundant on these muddy fishing grounds. In general, juvenile sharks (Triakidae and Squalidae) were usually discarded, and larger fish retained, whilst catsharks (Scyliorhinidae) were generally discarded. Temporal changes in discarding patterns are examined in relation to recent changes in management regulations, and potential implications of recent reform of the Common Fisheries Policy, in terms of discard bans, discussed.

title: Sawfish in the Mediterranean: vagrant species or an undetected case of regional extinction?

authors.affiliation: Stanford University, USA

abstract_text: The impact of humans on ocean ecosystems dates prehistoric times. However, only recently science has been able to describe these changes. For many animal populations, scientific observation has captured the epilogue of complex changes in abundance, distribution and interspecific interactions, and for sawfishes, their extinctions in many coastal zones. In the Mediterranean, a scant set of records raised doubts on whether sawfishes ever occurred in the region. It is currently suggested that sawfishes could not have inhabited the Mediterranean Sea because of the incongruent local oceanographic conditions with the known sawfish ecology. Here we will show the result of a bibliographic, archival and extinction analysis where we reconstructed the sawfish history in the Mediterranean. Between 1576 and 1956, we found 48 independent accounts on the occurrence of large and small-tooth sawfishes, including 23 documented catches. Sawfishes were mainly recorded in the western Mediterranean, in areas close to large rivers and light human impact. Most of the documented sawfishes were juveniles suggesting local parturition and the presence of resident populations. These populations, however, disappeared during the last five decades. We will discuss how our results challenge current assumptions on sawfish biogeography and ecology, highlight the importance of historical literature analyses in reconstructing baselines of animal populations, and call for a large-scale molecular and genetic characterization of sawfish exhibits present in Mediterranean and European museums.

title: Cryptic invaders from the Red Sea: the Dusky Shark in the Mediterranean

authors.affiliation: Institute of Evolution and Department of Evolutionary & Environmental Biology University of Haifa/ Israel Oceanographic and Limnological Research

abstract_text: Since the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869, many marine species have passed through from the Red Sea to the Mediterranean. This extensive phenomenon, known as Lessepsian migration, has so far resulted in the migration of over 400 species into the Levant Basin. Unlike other closely monitored marine megafauna such as marine mammals and sea turtles, little is known about shark populations in Israel. The Dusky Shark Carcharhinus obscurus is rarely found in most parts of the Mediterranean but is surprisingly common in Israel. In collaboration with Ecoocean organization, we aimed to explore the variability of Dusky Sharks off the Israeli coast and determine its origin by molecular techniques. Previous work on the Dusky Shark found the Indo-Pacific population to be genetically separated from the Atlantic one. We collected tissue samples of sharks caught by fishermen off the Israel Mediterranean coast. DNA was extracted and the mitochondrial control region (D-Loop) was sequenced. Results show that samples consisted of haplotypes from both the Atlantic and Indo-Pacific, indicating that Lessepsian migration of the Dusky Shark has occurred. Albeit rare, the Dusky Shark is indigenous in the Mediterranean, thus the usual definition of invasion does not apply. We address it as cryptic invasion, a term used for the phenomenon of individuals entering an existing population of the same species from a different biogeographic region. Identifying cryptic invasions is especially important in highly invaded regions such as the Mediterranean, and presents an especially difficult challenge in protecting the species while eradicating invaders and protecting the genetic diversity.

title: First results on migration behaviour of Leafscale Gulper Shark Centrophorus squamosus tagged in the Cantabrian Sea (NE Atlantic)

authors.affiliation: Instituto Español de Oceanografia (IEO)

abstract_text: Several Leafscale Gulper Sharks, Centrophorus squamosus were tagged with conventional tags in the North of Spain waters (Cantabrian Sea, NE Atlantic). In addition six specimens were tagged with satellite tags (PAT) in the Marine Protected Area (MPA) of Le Danois Bank (El Cachucho) in the central Cantabrian Sea in 2012 and 2013. Up to date data from three of these tags were recovered. The first one corresponded to a male of 104 cm which was 45 days at liberty and in this time it travelled about 246 miles towards the north east (French continental shelf) hypothetically following the continental slope at a mean depth of 900 m. The second shark, a male of 93 cm, spent almost 4 months (116 days) in which it moved 188 miles to the west (Galician coast) following the slope at a mean depth of 1200 m. Finally, the third one a male of 118 cm moved to the NW (Porcupine Bank) travelling approximately 550 miles during three months.

title: Mustelus asterias in the Netherlands

authors.affiliation: Sportvisserij Nederland

abstract_text: Sharkatag in Zeeland: Sharks and rays are an extremely rare (by)catch for anglers in the Dutch part of the North Sea. However, in 2010 skippers of deep sea angling charters, operating in the south of the Netherlands, noticed an unexpected increase in catches of the Starry Smoothhound Mustelus asterias. In 2011, the Royal Dutch Angling Organisation started a long-lasting tagging program together with the research institute IMARES and 15 skippers. After 3 years, nearly 1500 Starry Smoothhound Sharks have been tagged & released. Recaptures (22 so far) were sent to us by commercial fisherman from Belgium, France and the UK. Preliminary results show that the main migration route of the smoothhounds goes south through the Channel, and back again. It also seems that the large female smoothhound sharks gather in summer in a Nature 2000 area the "Oosterschelde", where they presumably give birth to their offspring. In addition to this on-going tagging program, the Angling Organisation organizes an event known as “Sharkatag”. The licensed skippers take 300 anglers, including policy makers and politicians, out to go shark-fishing. This event raises good media attention and is broadcast on the national news. The objective is primarily to generate more awareness amongst the general public and with policy-makers and politicians. Also anglers want the Dutch fisheries law to be re-evaluated on sharks & rays. The objective is to see that all sharks and rays caught in the Dutch part of the North Sea are released, since they are so rare, and important to the aquatic ecosystem.

title: Using biochemical markers to investigate the hidden lives of Whale Sharks

authors.affiliation: Marine Megafauna Foundation, Mozambique

abstract_text: Little is known about the long-term movements and feeding ecology of whale sharks away from coastal aggregation sites. Examining tissue biopsies using ‘biochemical tagging’ methods can provide information on their assimilated diet and movement patterns. Skin biopsies were collected from free-swimming Whale Sharks in Mozambique, Qatar, and Tanzania between 2011 and 2013. Stomach contents were collected from five stranded Whale Sharks in Mozambique and South Africa. Coastal zooplankton samples were collected at the surface and at 300m depth from Mozambique. Fatty acid profiles were assessed from the Mozambique biopsies alongside other planktivores and known or potential prey items. Carbon and nitrogen stable isotope ratios were determined from all skin biopsies. δN and δC values of skin biopsies differed by location, demonstrating consistent spatial segregation over the timescale of isotopic integration. This is supported by photo identification data which show negligible overlap of individuals between sites, and point to strong stock separation of whale sharks in the Western Indian Ocean. Fatty acid profiles of Whale Sharks were significantly different to all prey items. Several mesoand bathypelagic species showed among the highest similarity. Mysid shrimps dominated stomach contents numerically and by mass. Together this suggests Whale Sharks feed not only during daylight on surface zooplankton, but at night on demersal zooplankton and, on oceanic, and deep water zooplankton and fishes. Whale Sharks likely target multiple environments to feeding in the patchy prey fields of tropical systems, but appear to forage within a relatively limited latitudinal range.

title: Towards understanding Basking Shark Cetorhinus maximus connectivity – novel marker development and on-going genetic monitoring

authors.affiliation: University of Aberdeen

abstract_text: Classified on the IUCN Red List as ‘Vulnerable’ worldwide and ‘Endangered’ in the Northeast Atlantic (NEA) region, the filter-feeding basking shark, Cetorhinus maximus, is a marine conservation priority species in the UK. Although recent advances in satellite tracking have shed new light upon its movement and dispersal potential, little is known about Basking Shark connectivity, population size, or even basic life history traits. Following a century of commercial hunting, it has become vital for current conservation efforts to develop new tools to monitor numbers, migration units and gene flow within the NEA. Despite extensive migratory behaviour, Basking Sharks seasonally aggregate off Scotland, Ireland, southern England and the Isle of Man. As these aggregations could present a significant proportion of the global population, we have gathered long-term population samples using skin mucus swabs to allow monitoring of these key sites. Here, 13 novel, species-specific microsatellite genetic markers haven been developed and tested to allow first estimates of effective population sizes and genetic diversity. Furthermore, high-throughput RAD (restriction site – associated DNA) sequences are currently being filtered for hundreds of SNP (single nucleotide polymorphism) markers from the Basking Shark genome to provide more powerful, precise and robust tools for future monitoring. Individual identification is essential for estimates of animal movement and abundance and on-going genetic tagging will allow a range of hypotheses to be tested regarding annual site-fidelity, kinship and large-scale population structuring – parameters essential for meaningful stock assessments and management units in the light of offshore development and climate change.

title: Ambiguity, bycatch and demand - valid excuses for ineffective mobulid conservation?

authors.affiliation: Linnaeus University, Kalmar (Sweden) and The Manta Trust (UK)

abstract_text: The family Mobulidae comprises of two genera, Manta and Mobula, with 11 extant species worldwide and all are listed on the IUCN Red List as either “Vulnerable”, “Near Threatened” or “Data Deficient”. Limited data is available for these species and given that they have few natural predators, slow growth rates, low fecundity and late maturity, anthropogenic threats can have a severe impact on their global populations. Mobulid rays are landed as non-discarded by-catch in tuna gill-net fisheries across South Asia. The abundant species recorded are Mobula japanica and Mobula tarapacana, followed by Manta birostris and Mobula thurstoni. While Manta has some protection in certain regions and under the forthcoming CITES implementation, none of the Mobula species are adequately protected. This lack of protection is due to the scarcity of data which prevents a listing under multilateral treaties such as CITES. One critical factor currently affecting data collection are the similar external features among mobulids which often result in taxonomic ambiguities even in published scientific literature. This highlights the urgent necessity for a set of clear identification tools to help researchers fill in knowledge gaps, as the continuing difficulty of identification to species level is severely hindering our ability to understand more about these animals and recommend concrete conservation actions. With demand for mobulids growing due to the expanding international trade in their gill plates used in Traditional Chinese Medicine, it is imperative these rays are provided with some form of protection before their fragile populations are pushed beyond breaking point.

title: Wanted dead or alive! How tourism could save the manta ray

authors.affiliation: The Manta Trust, UK

abstract_text: In recent years manta rays have faced increasing threats from both targeted and by-catch fisheries due to a growing trade in their highly valued gill plates. Listed as “Vulnerable” on the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species, with life history traits including slow growth, late maturity and long pregnancies that usually result in the birth of a single pup, mantas are extremely susceptible to any consumptive exploitation. Manta rays are however, regarded as one of our oceans’ most charismatic species with many divers listing them high on their dive career bucket list. By harnessing this potential there are numerous opportunities that allow the public a very active role in saving these iconic species. Changing policy often requires scientists to take an interdisciplinary approach to providing evidence for reform. Tourism with mantas is one such example, with the direct economic impact of manta ray dive tourism estimated at US$140 million globally each year. When compared to an estimated US$5 million from the annual trade in manta gill plates, the alternative of simply swimming with mantas is an enormous economic incentive for protection. Tourism has also been used in conjunction with biological data in MPA designation affecting these species and has a vital role to play in funding ongoing management initiatives. Divers can also take a personal role, capturing images of each manta ray’s unique underside as they swim with them and subsequently working with researchers to identify animals they have encountered, providing vital data on manta populations, migrations and habitat use.

title: Multiple paternity in Lamnid sharks: implications for conservation management?

authors.affiliation: University of Aberdeen, UK

abstract_text: The vagility and intractability of elasmobranchs makes their reproductive interactions inherently difficult to study. Observations of mating behaviour are often rare or nonexistent, except for a few relatively tractable species with well-defined inshore nursery areas. The application of molecular methods to assign paternity is relatively recent in sharks, yet four out of eight extant orders have been shown to exhibit multiple paternity. We have used biparentally inherited microsatellite markers to extend these finding to another order of sharks, the Lamniformes. Here we report evidence of multiple paternity in three species from the family Lamnidae caught in the Pacific Ocean: the Great White, Carcharodon carcharias (off Japan and Taiwan), the Shortfin Mako, Isurus oxyrinchus (central south Pacific), and Porbeagle, Lamna nasus (south Pacific). Understanding the extent and prevalence of polyandry in large pelagic sharks could be of fundamental importance, as biological dogma dictates that multiply sired litters have a positive effect on the effective population size (NE), a parameter central to the philosophy of conservation biology.

title: Whale Shark provisioning: the case study of Oslob, Philippines

authors.affiliation: Physalus (NGO), Large Marine Vertebrate Project, Philippines

abstract_text: This represents the first description of the Whale Shark aggregation associated with the provisioning activities and tourism industry in the waters of Oslob, Philippines. Provisioning started in late 2011, and within the first year over 100,000 tourists were attracted to the site, transforming into one of the largest marine wildlife tourist attractions in South East Asia. Since March 2012 researchers collected photographic identification during 443 days of surveys, 200h of shark behavioural observations and 1000h of dive profiles from TDR tags as well as daily observations of tourists’ and operators’ compliance with local and national laws and 500 tourist satisfaction questionnaires. Daily sightings ranged from 2 to 23 different animals in the interaction area (mean=11.14). A total of 109 males, 15 females and 11 sharks of undetermined sex were described. Resighting (>1d) was observed in 66.7% of the individuals. Five animals were present for >300d (n=443) in the interaction area and nine were successfully matched across regional hotspots including Donsol and Southern Leyte. Whale Sharks are present in the interaction area year round, with a maximum of 46 different animals present in the month of June 2012 and May 2013 (monthly average: 28.9). Although the benefits for the community and regional economy are undeniable, evidence of behavioural modification, extended residency time and thermal stress related to the extended permanence in shallow water, suggests that the impact of the provisioning needs to be further investigated and highlights the need of a proper management plan for the tourism industry.

title: Seaquest Southwest Basking Shark Project

authors.affiliation: Cornwall Wildlife Trust

abstract_text: The Seaquest Basking Shark Project is an effort-based annual survey of basking shark sightings carried out in Cornwall by a large team of volunteers. The sightings scheme aims to; Maintain a database with information on the number of sightings recorded at Hella Point each year; Collect and analyse sightings data to improve knowledge of Basking Shark distribution, behaviour and threats around the coast of Cornwall; Raise public awareness about basking sharks and the threats they face. The Seaquest Basking Shark Project was launched by Cornwall Wildlife Trust in 2008 and ran until 2012, collecting over 3270 hours of effort data.
