title: A regional dorsal fin-based population estimate for White Sharks Carcharodon carcharias in Gansbaai, South Africa

authors.affiliation: The Dyer Island Conservation Trust, South Africa

abstract_text: Gansbaai, South Africa is reputed to host the world’s largest remaining population of White Sharks, yet no regional estimates existed for the area prior to this study and the only previous regional population estimate of White Sharks in South Africa relied on culled animals. We used dorsal fin photographs (fin IDs) collected during commercial cage diving trips to identify individual white sharks from January 2007 – December 2011, totalling 4120 hours of observer effort without seasonal paucity. We utilized the computer programme DARWIN to catalogue and match fin IDs of individuals. Of 1682 fin IDs used, 532 unique individuals were identified. Population size was determined using the open-population POPAN parameterisation in Program MARK, which estimated the superpopulation size at 908 (95% confidence interval 808–1008). Dorsal fins were found to be an inconsistent mark-recapture feature, as individual fins were found to change over time, which was not related to the size or sex of sharks. Our estimated population size is larger than those described at other aggregation areas of the species, yet is comparable to a previous regional population estimate conducted 16 years prior using animals caught in KwaZulu Natal shark nets. This suggests the species has not made a marked recovery since being nationally protected in 1991. As such, additional international protection may prove vital for the long-term conservation of this threatened species. This study was recently published in PLOS ONE: http://www.plosone.org/article/info%3Adoi%2F10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0066035
session_name: Session 2B: Manta Rays, Whale Sharks, Basking Sharks, and White Sharks

title: Using videography to understand the effects of large marine reserves on pelagic, migratory species

authors.affiliation: Zoological Society of London

abstract_text: Large, pelagic predators, such as sharks, are fundamental to marine ecosystem health, but have been seriously impacted by industrial fisheries, and populations of a number of species have declined significantly. As such, the development of methods that can be used to establish baselines and deliver on-going monitoring of pelagic species using safe, non-destructive, low-cost and transferable technology is essential for improving their management. Stereo baited remote underwater video systems (BRUVS) are an established survey technique for monitoring fish and in 2011, we began adapting BRUVs for use in the pelagic realm. The adaptation of this technique to the pelagic environment aimed to document the diversity, abundance and size structure of mobile pelagic predators, including sharks. Sea trials of these units have now taken place off Dirk Hartog Island, Western Australia, and the Chagos Marine Reserve and results will be presented. This video technique is presently being progressed to develop units that record data over extended time periods using still photography, videography and a suite of environmental sensors that would be satellite-linked and allow immediate remote access to data. This development would pose a number of technological challenges, and a number of lab and aquarium-based trials were carried out in 2012-2013, prior to the first field trials of a monitoring buoy which housed still cameras in Chagos in February 2013. Preliminary findings of these trials will be presented. It is hoped that data gathered from these unit will address management and legislative issues related to conservation of sharks globally.

title: Exploring ENGO perspectives on shark conservation through narrative analysis

authors.affiliation: University of Leeds

abstract_text: Within social science studies of conservation, it is increasingly acknowledged that the way in which key stakeholders understand, prioritise, articulate and communicate issues can have a significant influence on the way in which such issues are managed. This is particularly important in areas of high uncertainty, such as the conservation of migratory marine species that include sharks, skates, rays and chimaeras. Environmental non-governmental organisations (ENGOs) have a key role in how shark conservation issues are understood, prioritised and addressed in both policy and public arenas. This research report uses six case studies to illustrate how ENGOs perceive and frame shark conservation issues and how they present their evidence and arguments. It finds that a contested mix of science, moral and economic arguments are used across organisations and that three broad narratives are deployed by ENGOs, focusing on sustainability, shark finning, and ecosystemic and intrinsic species value. By gaining a better understanding of the way in which these influential ENGOs articulate shark conservation issues, along with the factors that influence this, we are able to gain insight into the opportunities and challenges this may pose for policy-making and conservation management. The research also identifies changes that appear to be occurring in the way in which shark conservation issues are articulated, which may have further policy implications into the future.

title: Shark nursery identification on a shoestring without getting wet: evidence for the regional importance of the threatened Tigris-Euphrates system to Bull Sharks

authors.affiliation: RSK Environment Ltd/Bangor University

abstract_text: The identification of nursery areas is recognised as a key priority for elasmobranch conservation, yet the logistics and cost of obtaining the field survey data required to fulfil the strict criteria of a nursery can be prohibitive. Although a relatively well-studied species worldwide, the ecology of the Bull Shark in the Tigris-Euphrates river system in Iraq, Kuwait and Iran is poorly known, a situation not helped by three decades of warfare and border tensions. A range of data is presented, including from anecdotal and historical sources, which build support for a Bull Shark nursery of potentially regional importance. This nursery warrants further investigation, especially in light of the many environmental pressures on the area.

title: Core habitat use of an apex predator in a complex marine landscape

authors.affiliation: Dyer Island Conservation Trust, South Africa

abstract_text: Manual acoustic telemetry was used to describe core habitat use of white sharks in the complex marine landscape of the Dyer Island and Geyser Rock system near Gansbaai, South Africa. Home range estimates and swimming pattern analyses were compared to patterns established at Mossel Bay, another aggregation area roughly 300 km to the east. Traditional home range estimates used in Mossel Bay did not account for movement or barriers, and as a result were biased towards resting areas. We found that adapting a movement-based kernel density estimate (MKDE) resolved these issues and produced more accurate results. At Dyer Island and Geyser Rock, shark daytime habitat use was adjacent to the seal colony, with slow rates of movement, non-linear swimming patterns and small activity areas. At night, rates of movement increased as sharks travelled further from the islands into deeper waters. MKDEs revealed four focal areas of habitat use; a channel between the two islands, an area to the south of the seal colony, another area near a kelp feature to the south-west of the seal colony and a reef system to the north-west. These results differed significantly from patterns at Mossel Bay, where sharks were found to only approach the seal colony during the hours of dawn and dusk and spent the majority of their time patrolling distant reefs. Possible reasons for these differences are discussed within. This study is the first to make use of MKDEs in a complex marine landscape.

title: The Great Eggcase Hunt: ten years on

authors.affiliation: The Shark Trust, UK

abstract_text: Spawning and nursery grounds are ecologically-important habitats, yet surprisingly little is known about the locations of such sites for skate species (Rajidae) and oviparous sharks in the North Atlantic. These grounds may be identified by the presence of large numbers of mature females or by a high density of eggcases on the sea floor. However, empty eggcases which have washed ashore can also provide an easily accessible source of information on the broad distribution and diversity of egglaying elasmobranch populations, although the site where an eggcase is found is not necessarily indicative of where it was laid. The Great Eggcase Hunt (GEH) is a Shark Trust public awareness and recording project that aims to discover where different species of skate and oviparous shark lay their eggs. Initially, it was driven by evidence of declining populations and the lack of species-specific recording, which demonstrated the need for an increased understanding of all aspects of life history strategy: the GEH represents the public aspect of this work. Eggcase taxonomy featured heavily during the early days of the project, as limited published information was available on the egglaying phase of the skate life cycle, despite many being commercially important species. Now in its tenth year, over 35,000 individual eggcases, representing 13 species of skate and shark species, have been recorded to the project. In a changing landscape for elasmobranch management, the GEH continues to provide a valuable source of information which has the potential to feed into management measures, while also operating as an educational tool to raise awareness of the presence and diversity of elasmobranchs in British waters and further afield.

title: Migration patterns of an apex marine predator targetting pelagic prey

authors.affiliation: Plymouth University, UK

abstract_text: Migration strategies are an adaptive response to temporal variation in availability and location of resources. Migrations of highly connected predators are of particular interest given their central role in maintaining ecosystem stability. Despite a traditional focus on terrestrial species, advances in remote telemetry have facilitated descriptions of migrations in various marine predators. However, the underlying motivations for migration and whether they are partial or not often remain overlooked. Consequently this study aimed to determine the factors driving migration in an apex marine predator: the Tiger Shark Galeocerdo cuvier. Satellite-derived movement data from the Northwest Atlantic revealed seasonal, round-trip migrations of 4,000 km between insular regions in winter and offshore pelagic areas in summer. These migrations were partial, with the majority of observed migrations undertaken by mature males. Combining these findings with stomach data and existing literature indicates the motivation behind summer migrations is likely linked to foraging on juvenile Loggerhead Turtles Caretta caretta, before returning to mate at breeding grounds in winter. Migrating to target turtles may be an adaptation for avoiding competition with other large, sympatric, predators that favour teleosts and cephalopods.

title: Sharks across the pond: divergence and convergence in US-EU elasmobranch conservation

authors.affiliation: Shark Advocates International, USA

abstract_text: The European Union (EU) and the United States (US) are significant players in global shark fishing and policy. The US has championed shark safeguards for two decades and now boasts several success stories. EU shark and ray policies have improved markedly in recent years, and are now in some cases more precautionary than those of the US. For Spurdog, Porbeagle, and skates, Europe has a much longer fishing history and provides the demand that drives US fisheries. For these and other elasmobranch species, current management strategies and results differ, with approaches to deepsea sharks being the most divergent. Both entities have taken the same unfortunate path regarding smoothhounds: allowing targeted fishing without population assessment or limits. The EU finning ban -- long notorious as the world’s worst -- is now in line with best practice (fins remain attached through landing) and more stringent than those in the US, where such policies first emerged. US promotion of international fins-attached policies have recently been boosted by EU partnership. The US and EU have collaborated toward international safeguards for pelagic sharks and clashed on those for skates. Both parties are leaders in advancing and implementing shark and ray conservation through the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) and the Convention on Migratory Species (CMS). These converging and diverging policies leave significant deficiencies and opportunities on both sides of the Atlantic. Recommendations for change will be offered.

title: The two T’s, tracking and taxonomy: implications of recent research findings for the management of White Sharks and Spurdogs in New Zealand waters and beyond

authors.affiliation: Department of Conservation, The University of Auckland

abstract_text: High tech versus low tech, cutting edge versus quaint and outdated. These are arguably widely held views of modern electronic tracking and taxonomic studies of elasmobranchs respectively. But which has the most influence on management? Overviews of ongoing research on the movements and habitat preferences of White Shark’s Carcharodon carcharias and the taxonomy of spurdogs Squalus spp. in New Zealand waters will be presented with this question in mind. The rapid taxonomic approach adopted to identify new chondrichthyan taxa in Australasia has proved to be a powerful means of addressing the pressing need to clarify the taxonomic status of a large number of exploited species in the region. Personal observations on the application of this approach, including the combination of morphological and molecular analyses to identify and diagnose species, will also be provided.

title: Quantifying the impact of environmental variables upon Blue Shark Prionace glauca Catch-Per-Unit-Effort in the Western English Channel

authors.affiliation: University of Southampton, UK

abstract_text: The North Atlantic Blue Shark Prionace glauca population has declined significantly in recent decades, due to increasing fishing pressure driven by demand for fins. This highlights the need for greater understanding of P. glauca biology and ecology, and its interaction with fisheries, to prevent further declines. This research quantified the impact of environmental variables on P. glauca Catch-Per-Unit-Effort (CPUE) in a recreational fishery in the Western English Channel, using Generalized Additive Models (GAM). Surface chlorophyll a concentration (CHL) caused 27.5% of the deviance in the GAM response variable, CPUE, and increasing CHL positively affected CPUE up to a peak at 1.77mg m-3, likely due to higher productivity supporting greater prey biomass. Conversely, tidal mixing front density explained only 5% of model deviance, and was negatively associated with CPUE. However, time-lagged front density positively influenced CPUE, and explained 12.6% of model deviance, suggesting a delay between the evolution of frontal features and the subsequent accumulation of productivity and attraction of higher trophic-level consumers, i.e. P. glauca. Sea Surface Temperature (SST) only accounted for 1.4% of GAM deviance, with maximum CPUE occurring at 16.7⁰C, reflecting thermal preferences of this species, and supporting previous data for the influence of SST on P. glauca CPUE. This knowledge of environmental preferences and their impact upon the likelihood of P. glauca being caught in fisheries, may be combined with information on migratory movements and population dynamics in the North Atlantic population, offering potential for the creation of effective, integrated fisheries management models for this species.

title: Big catch, little sharks: Peruvian small-scale longline fisheries likely to be unsustainable

authors.affiliation: University of Exeter, UK & Pro Delphinus

abstract_text: Shark take, driven by vast demand for their meat and fins is increasing. We set out to gain insights into the impact of small-scale longline fisheries in Peru. Onboard observers were used to document catch from 145 longline fishing trips originating from southern Peru. Fishing effort is divided into two seasons; targeting dolphinfish Dec to Feb), and sharks (Mar to Nov). A total of 16,610 sharks were observed caught, with 11,166 identified to species level. Of these 70.6% were Blue Sharks Prionace glauca, 28.4% Shortfin Mako Sharks Isurus oxyrinchus, and 1% were other species. Mean ± SD catch per unit effort of 36.8 ± 11.9 sharks per 1,000 hooks was recorded from positive sets (93.7% of total sets) during the shark season and 6.6 ± 9.7 sharks per 1,000 hooks were caught in positive sets (24.4% of total sets) in the dolphinfish season. An average of 83.7% of sharks caught (74.7% Blue Sharks; 93.3% mako sharks) were deemed sexually immature and under the legal minimum landing size. Since these growing fisheries operate along the entire Peruvian coast, we conclude that their continued expansion, along with ineffective legislative approaches resulting in removal of immature individuals, has the potential to threaten the sustainability of the fishery, its target species and ecosystem. There is a need for novel management strategies to alleviate the pressure on sharks while maintaining fisher livelihoods.

title: Habitat-use, foraging behaviour and fisheries overlap of Shortfin Mako sharks Isurus oxyrinchus in the North Atlantic

authors.affiliation: CIBIO – Center for Research in Biodiversity and Genetic Resources, Portugal

abstract_text: The Shortfin Mako Isurus oxyrinchus is a highly migratory, pelagic species with a circumglobal distribution. However, despite reported population declines prompting an urgent need for information relevant to conservation, very little is known about its biology, including movement patterns, behaviour and habitat preferences. As a precautionary approach it has recently been proposed by ICCAT that fishing mortality of mako sharks should not be increased, because the precise location and composition of catches is lacking and, as such, it is challenging to determine if the observed variability in CPUE trends is related to variations in the area targeted. This study aimed to determine the movements and behaviour of satellite-linked mako sharks to identify (i) preferred habitat from remotely sensed environmental fields and (ii) critical habitat from the extent of overlap with tracked longlining vessels. Tagged sharks (#15) exhibited different movement patterns, including a trans-Atlantic migration ~3500 km into western Iberia waters. Nonetheless, space-use of mako sharks appears highly influenced by the North Atlantic Current – Labrador Current Convergence Zone (NAC-LCCZ) with the majority of sharks remaining or moving into this area, which is characterised by high prevalence of oceanic fronts. Mako Sharks also displayed wide ranging vertical movements (usually to depths below 1000 m), with shifts in thermal and depth-use patterns seemingly correlated with environmental variation. Importantly, mako sharks had more than 76% of their range overlapped by longliners and, although fishing effort was highly heterogeneous, the NAC-LCCZ area was also heavily targeted by longlining vessels.

title: Tracking migration routes in pelagic shark populations through dynamic isoscapes

authors.affiliation: University of Southampton, NOCS, UK

abstract_text: Highly migratory, pelagic sharks have declined in abundance by >90% in the last 25 years, largely due to unsustainable fishing and by-catch. Managing and conserving the remaining populations requires a complete understanding of their spatial ecology. Migration routes in pelagic sharks, however, are difficult to reconstruct, particularly at a population level. Despite recent advances in satellite tagging technologies, smart tags are still expensive and relatively few, large individuals can be studied. In terrestrial ecosystems, knowledge of the spatial ecology of highly migratory organisms, such as birds, insects and mammals, has been revolutionised by natural stable isotope markers. Location and movements are reconstructed indirectly, by relating the tissue isotopic composition of an animal to known geographic variations in the isotopic composition of the local food web or environment (isotopic baseline). In marine settings, isotopic baselines are highly dynamic, and the nature, extent and implications of baseline variations are poorly known, limiting the confidence that can be placed in ecological inferences based on isotopic datasets. We have developed a mechanistic, predictive modelling approach to produce dynamic maps of baseline variations (isoscapes). Here we apply these isoscapes to track migration routes in pelagic shark populations from literature-derived and newly measured tissue isotopic compositions. We believe that, when baseline variations are known or predictable, stable isotopes markers may be as effective at revealing migratory behaviour in pelagic sharks as they have been in terrestrial birds, insects and mammals.

title: Genetic population structure among Atlantic nurseries of the highly mobile oceanic Blue Shark Prionace glauca

authors.affiliation: CIBIO – Center for Research in Biodiversity and Genetic Resources, Portugal

abstract_text: The Blue Shark Prionace glauca is a cosmopolitan oceanic shark that is heavily targeted as a by-catch of tuna and billfish fisheries, particularly in the Atlantic Ocean. Concerns for the exploitation status of this species have been raised following the detection of declines in Blue Shark abundance in the North Atlantic. Despite its high fishing mortality, Blue Shark stock structure is still poorly understood and based almost exclusively on data from tag-recapture studies. In order to help clarify the stock structure of Blue Sharks, we applied molecular markers, e.g. nuclear microsatellites and mitochondrial control region sequences, to study the patterns of genetic population structure within the Atlantic. The high dispersal ability of P. glauca, coupled to its complex movement patterns and spatial segregation by sex and size, require a carefully designed sampling strategy in order to clearly delineate the putative stocks. We have sampled small juveniles (< 2 yr) at each of three reported Atlantic Blue Shark nurseries, i.e. western Iberia, Azores and South Africa, thus targeting the least mobile component of the population and avoiding sampling of highly mobile adults of unknown origin. Our data show significant genetic heterogeneity among nurseries at both nuclear and mitochondrial markers, but also suggest a signal of temporal structure within as well as across nurseries. These results raise additional questions regarding the existence of distinct reproductive units that may co-occur in time and space within Atlantic waters, and the possibility of annual variability in the composition of the breeding component of the populations.

title: Are we doing the right thing to save sharks and rays? How to plan for conservation success

authors.affiliation: International Union for the Conservation of Nature/ Department of Biological Sciences, Simon Fraser University, Canada

abstract_text: There is too little money to save all the species we want to save. So how should we go about figuring out which sharks and rays to save? We could do this in an idiosyncratic manner and just save our favourite study species. But then the oceans would be a much poorer place if we only saved the 20 or so most-studied sharks and rays out of the 1100 known chondrichthyans. We can take an evidence-based approach to conservation planning. Now that we have Red List Assessments for all of the world’s sharks, rays and chimaeras we can use this information to set conservation priorities. Here, we describe how we identify those families that are at most risk of extinction. We then describe how we used the IUCN conservation strategic planning process to identify those action and locations that are most likely to contribution to effective conservation of Sawfishes. We conclude with plans to develop conservation strategies the manta and devil rays and the Angelshark Squatina squatina.

title: Can microtextural analyses be used as a dietary discriminator in sharks?

authors.affiliation: University of Leicester, UK

abstract_text: Determining the dietary preferences and trophic niches of elasmobranchs can be difficult, yet this information is essential for ecological analysis and successful conservation. Stomach contents analyses have traditionally been used but this approach has many drawbacks, and requires large sample sizes to be reliable. This and other issues make stomach contents analyses problematic for many elasmobranch species and thus it is essential that alternative methods are developed to quantify diet. Quantitative microtextural analysis of tooth wear is one such approach to dietary discrimination. Until recently its application was restricted to terrestrial mammals, but it is now known to be a powerful tool for analysis of trophic niche and dietary change in fishes. Microtextural analysis of shark teeth has never been attempted, and the hypothesis that it is correlated with diet, feeding and/or trophic niche thus remains untested. Here we present the results of a proof-of-concept study designed to investigate the potential of microwear analysis for dietary discrimination in elasmobranchs. Using the Port Jackson Shark, Heterodontus portusjacksoni, analysis of variation in sub-micron scale microtextures within a tooth, between teeth within an individual, and between individuals, suggests that a dietary signal is preserved. These results indicate that microtextural analysis provides a new approach to investigating diet in sharks. Future work will apply these methods to other elasmobranchs, including endangered and lesser known modern species, to determine ontogenetic, geographical and evolutionary changes in diet.

title: Shark and other fish eye lenses – a window to cryptic life history behaviours

authors.affiliation: University of Southampton, UK

abstract_text: Traditionally, tagging studies provide information relating to the distribution and movement patterns of pelagic sharks. Electronic tags, however, are expensive, may have low return rates, and cannot be attached to small juveniles. Incrementally grown tissues offer an alternative biochemical method to study ecology retrospectively. Otoliths, for example, contain a wealth of information pertaining to the age, growth and whole life, including juvenile, ecology of a species. The crystalline lens in the vertebrate eye also grows incrementally, but this structure has received relatively little analytical attention. Unlike otoliths, lenses are proteinaceous structures formed by fibre cell addition and subsequent progressive dehydration towards the core. They are acellular, and are not remodelled or replaced. Consequently, lenses have the potential to serve as a chronological record of biochemical information allowing examination of ontogenetic movement patterns, migration and juvenile ecology in a wide range of functional groups, including elasmobranchs. Here we report pilot data examining the dietary ecology and movement/migration of the Porbeagle Shark Lamna nasus using stable isotope analyses from sequential samples of eye lens tissue. We explore the potential for eye lenses as a log of life-long diet and spatial ecology, and compare their role as biochemical host tissues with vertebrae. We use the recovered diet and migration data to reconstruct feeding and movement ecology in juvenile Porbeagle Sharks and compare inferences from stable isotope data with those from physical tagging.

title: Quantification of metabolic rate in free ranging elasmobranch species by means of tri-axial accelerometry

authors.affiliation: Bimini Biological Field Station Foundation, Bahamas

abstract_text: Determining accurate field metabolic rate (FMR) is important for quantifying a species’ impact on the ecosystem, estimating effects of their removal on lower trophic levels and producing reliable bioenergetics models for fisheries management. This multi-institutional project aims to determine FMR in three elasmobranch species with contrasting energetic requirements: the sedentary, benthic Nurse Shark Ginglymostoma cirratum, intermediate Lemon Shark Negaprion brevirostris and active, obligate ram ventilating Blacktip Shark Carcharhinus limbatus. Since activity-based energy expenditure is likely to be the largest component of FMR in sharks, their fine-scale activity levels can be used as a proxy for relative FMR at varying temperatures. This study uses animal-borne, tri-axial acceleration loggers that measure dynamic acceleration from body movement in the three orthogonal planes (heave, surge and sway) at a rate of up to 30Hz. To date, useable acceleration data has been collected around the Bimini Islands from four free-living nurse sharks (<90cm TL; one winter, three summer) and 14 Lemon Sharks (four winter, 10 summer). Preliminary analysis for N. brevirostris data allowed us to characterize behaviours such as resting, steady and fast-start swimming. These activities showed an average of 10.83% ± 5.92 (mean ± SD) and 15.74% ± 5.64 time spent resting during summer and winter respectively; 89.04% ± 5.90 and 84.17% ± 5.65 for steady swimming; 0.12% ±0.04 and 0.08% ±0.03 for fast-start swimming. This study is still continuing but once complete is expected to demonstrate a revolutionary technique in determining FMR in marine predators, a thus far unattained goal.

title: Neophilia and boldness in juvenile Lemon Shark: are novel object answer and frightening stimulus reaction relevant behavior indicators to shark personality?

authors.affiliation: Bimini Biological Field Station, Bahamas

abstract_text: Recent interest for personality has led to an increasing number of studies on a variety of animals regarding this topic. While we know how to investigate this phenomenon in certain species, it takes creativity and imagination to test for personality in others never studied before. Here we focus on the juvenile Lemon Shark, Negaprion brevirostris, a species that has never been tested regarding that matter. We looked at different personality traits, features of a personality, and the potential links which exist in between them. Correlated traits are referred to as behavioral syndromes, and this notion is steadily gaining interest in the scientific community. We conducted two experiments to find signs of personality in this key predator: the novel object experiment and that of the frightening stimulus. Since we have no previous reference, we assume that they are measuring for neophilia and boldness respectively. Our aim is to determine whether this assumption is verified. In order to do so, we compare different shark populations which will enable us to confirm the so-far-putative trait associated with each experiment. Our findings suggest that neophilia in sharks tested with the novel object experiment is consistent, which is a clear sign of personality. Then, some potential behavioral syndromes have been discovered, even though further investigations are needed to assert them. Personality can explain some behaviors which don’t seem adaptive at first, and could, in the end, be a deciding tool regarding both habitat and stock management.

title: Bioaccumulation of trace metals and organochlorines in North-East Atlantic Porbeagle Sharks Lamna nasus

authors.affiliation: Centre for Environment, Fisheries and Aquaculture Science (CEFAS), UK

abstract_text: In marine ecosystem management there is a growing concern over the levels of trace metals and organochlorines (OC), due to their bio-accumulative nature at high trophic levels. Numerous studies around the coast of UK have looked into the accumulation of trace metals and organochlorine (OC) contaminants in the blubber and liver tissues of various marine mammal species. However the impact of such contaminants on the fitness of other top predators such as Porbeagle Sharks remains relatively unknown. In this study, we describe the bioaccumulation of trace metals and organochlorines within the dorsal muscle and liver tissue of 12 Porbeagles (mean length 169cm, range 117 - 245cm), by-caught during commercial gill netting operations within the Celtic Sea. Our results show levels of trace metals such as zinc (6.78 ± 3.18 mg/kg ww), and arsenic (10.00 ± 3.63 mg/kg ww), to be relatively high, together with significant levels of cadmium (7.2 mg/kg ww), observed in one individual suggestive of potential dietary influences upon prey such as squid. For organochlorine contaminants HCB, α-HCH, γ-HCH and p,p'-TDE, all were found to be below detectable limits (0.25 ug/kg ww) of quantitation (LOQ), which given the lipophilic nature of these contaminants may be accounted for by the notable lean lipid content (<1-2%), of the dorsal muscle tissue. PCBs and dieldrin were detected in all 12 animals (at 0.85 ± 0.61 ∑PCB mg/kg lipid and 0.04 ± 0.01 mg/kg lipid respectively), with PBDEs, p,p’-DDT and p,p’-DDE detected in 8, 2 and 11 animals, respectively.

title: Adaptive divergence in the Thornback Ray Raja clavata

authors.affiliation: University of Aberdeen, UK

abstract_text: The Thornback Ray Raja clavata is common to the varying environments of European waters. Although its dispersal is limited, it occupies a range of habitats along a considerable latitudinal gradient, factors which may contribute to genetic differentiation and local adaptation. Studies employing solely neutral molecular markers, whilst usefully determining population history and connectivity, may overlook important functional traits under strong environmental selection such as body shape, colouration and armour. Given that natural selection acts on the phenotype, genetic variation in quantitative traits, such as these, is a prerequisite for a successful response to changing environmental conditions. The preservation of such diversity has perceivable benefits for species conservation yet the geography of adaptive variation remains poorly understood in marine systems. Understanding how European skates and rays interact with their environment provides much needed information to assist with defining appropriate fisheries management units to aid sustainability and conservation. We have contrasted the variation of distinct morphological characteristics with neutral genetic divergence in a number of populations to assess the extent of evolutionary adaptation at both local and broader geographic scales, and discuss the implications of this for stock management and the preservation of functional diversity.

title: Population genetic structure and phylogeography of the Smallspotted Catshark Scyliorhinus canicula in European waters

authors.affiliation: University of Calgary/ University of Salford

abstract_text: The Smallspotted Catshark Scyliorhinus canicula is distributed in the continental shelf and uppermost slope waters of the North Eastern Atlantic; from Norway and the British Isles south to Senegal, including the Mediterranean Sea. It is considered to be the most abundant catshark in European inshore waters. In the Atlantic, it is often caught as bycatch in demersal fisheries, with a growing commercial importance through its use as whelk bait, whilst it is targeted for consumption in the Mediterranean. In this study we used 526 specimens collected from eleven localities to assess population genetic structure by examining control region mtDNA and microsatellite diversities. Both markers showed similar genetic signatures, with significant separation of catshark populations across the Mediterranean, weak genetic differentiation of Portuguese sharks, and extensive gene flow within the rest of the North Atlantic. Our data imply that distinct evolutionary significant units occur within the Mediterranean, whereas little genetic sub-division could be recognised in the North East Atlantic. Therefore, like many coastal species, the Smallspotted Catshark should be managed regionally.

title: Endothermy in sharks: a Comparative Transcriptome Approach

authors.affiliation: Imperial College London & University of Aberdeen

abstract_text: The Shortfin Mako shark is one of the fastest living sharks and along with all other members of the Lamnidae family, shows the unique ability to maintain a super-predatory lifestyle in cool waters. Despite the energetic cost, lamnid sharks are endothermic, where some are able to sustain a body temperature 10°C higher than that of the ambient temperature. This adaptation to produce and retain metabolic heat has inevitably enabled their successful niche expansion. Shark endothermy has been characterized at a physiological level yet its molecular underpinnings have received little attention. Both functional evolutionary innovation in protein structure, or regulation of gene expression, could result in greater metabolic activities causing endothermy. Evidence for strong adaptive evolution in conserved metabolic genes is rare, although has been documented where selection pressure for enhanced aerobic metabolism has been particularly strong. Due to the extreme cost of maintaining an elevated body temperature in a marine environment, lamnid sharks represent an interesting group to investigate molecular evolutionary adaptation. Here, we used revolutionary RNA-seq to sequence the muscle transcriptomes of two endothermic sharks: the Shortfin Mako and Porbeagle, and their ectothermic sister species the Sandtiger Shark. Functional annotation and analysis of positive selection reveal that it is likely endothermy in sharks is governed by changes in gene expression and/or membrane modification. This work represents a substantial increase in available shark sequence data that will prove useful in light of an up-and-coming elasmobranch reference genome for assessing how sharks evolve and cope with ecological and environmental challenges.

title: A European Shark Tagging Programme and the importance of volunteers in ongoing scientific research into shark populations

authors.affiliation: Scottish Sea angling Conservation Network/Aberdeen University

abstract_text: Many of Scotland’s native elasmobranchs are now considered severely depleted as a result of overfishing and other anthropogenic pressures. The Scottish Shark Tagging Programme (SSTP) is a mark/recapture scheme established to record data on Scotland’s elasmobranch species. The voluntary nature of the SSTP drastically reduces the labour and financial costs normally associated with shark research allowing the SSTP to compile a database of over 6,500 records spanning a period of several decades. This has provided a much needed insight into the movements of sharks throughout European waters highlighting the need for data collection along entire migration routes to ensure suitable management as some species pass through the territorial waters of several EU member states. The SSTP has shown volunteer anglers can be a valuable data source, capable of contributing to and working with Government bodies such as Marine Scotland Science. SSTP data has served as a foundation for two government research projects and two PhD studentships researching the spatial ecology of elasmobranchs. The SSTP model has now been adopted by other EU member states in the hope of providing information on the cross-border movements of highly migratory species. This effort has provided valuable insight into shared stocks as well as raising the profile of sea angling and the role of citizen science in marine conservation. This presentation focuses on the importance of volunteer participation and the data collected by the SSTP as well as looking forwards towards the benefits of a European shark tagging program to ensure shared marine resources are managed sustainably.

title: Using Fishers’ ecological knowledge to assess the status and cultural importance of sawfish in Guinea-Bissau

authors.affiliation: Benguela Research & Training Noé Conservation

abstract_text: Sawfishes have declined dramatically in West Africa and may be extinct throughout much of their range. Guinea-Bissau is considered to be one of the last remaining places in West Africa where sawfish persist. Fishers’ Ecological Knowledge (FEK) can provide valuable baseline data, which can be used to direct scientific studies in situations where information is scarce or lacking and can also provide insight into local attitudes towards species of interest. Interview surveys were used to collect data on the past and current range of sawfishes within Guinea-Bissau waters, perceived causes of the decline amongst fishermen, and the local cultural importance of this species. Data were collected from 274 respondents, of whom 85% could identify a sawfish from an image. The majority of respondents reported to have last seen a sawfish in the 1980s, although this varied considerably by region, and 30% of respondents in the south had seen or captured sawfishes in the past decade. Overfishing or excessive fishing pressure was most frequently cited as a perceived cause for sawfish decline, followed by shark finning and overseas fishermen. The sawfish is primarily of cultural importance in the Bijagos Islands, where it is central to many traditional ceremonies. Information on recent catches will be useful for directing future work to locate and protect remaining sawfish in Guinea-Bissau. Insight gained into the cultural importance of sawfishes to Bissau-Guineans and their concerns in relation to the sustainability of their local fishery resources will be important to consider when designing management strategies.

title: Shark ByWatch UK – regional bycatch awareness of sharks and rays in the southern North Sea

authors.affiliation: Centre for Environment, Fisheries and Aquaculture Science (CEFAS), UK

abstract_text: Shark By-Watch UK, a forward thinking pilot project, supported by scientists, but led by fishermen, aims to increase knowledge of shark and ray by-catch and discarding in the inshore fisheries of the southern North Sea (ICES area IVc), to better inform policy decisions and improve fishing practices that will support long-term sustainable shark and ray fisheries. Through dedicated engagement workshops, regional inshore fishermen have been able to voice the important issues to them, which have become the foundation of this research programme. As a result the project has taken forward two industry focussed Case Studies 1) The current status of the Thames Estuary Thornback Ray and lost and 2) Forgotten shark and ray fisheries off East Anglia. Strong partnerships between coastal fishermen and scientists have been developed to collect and share data through engagement workshops, fishery-dependent shark and ray field surveys, mark ID tagging programmes, dedicated website and social media. To date, field data have been collected for over 6000 individual sharks and rays, highlighting their potential abundance and commercial value to local inshore fleets off the coast of East Anglia. The project has gained significant attention from Defra Fisheries Minister Richard Benyon, shark policy advisors and regional Inshore Fisheries Conservation Authority (IFCA) organisations who support such a proof of concept within the Shark By-Watch UK pilot study and avidly see the need for such work to be rolled out at a nationwide scale to help provide evidence and support for future management issues regarding “live” discarding measures around the UK.

title: Managing a captive species – Raja undulata

authors.affiliation: SEA LIFE Weymouth

abstract_text: The Undulate Ray Raja undulata is classified on the IUCN redlist as ‘Endangered’. This has led to the landing of the undulate ray in UK waters to be prohibited since 2009 while wild populations recover. In captivity, it is a great ‘poster species’ allowing aquariums to engage with the public regarding issues such as overfishing and habitat degradation. There is a healthy aquarium population, so over the last 3 years Displays Development Department at Weymouth SEA LIFE Park have been leading a managed UK breeding program of the species to ensure the future of the undulate ray on public display. This raises the challenge of sustaining a genetically healthy and stable population without the option of introducing wild caught specimens from UK waters. Involving aquaria throughout the UK and coordinated through the BIAZA native ray and skate focus group the project is now also monitoring the European captive population via EAZA. This presentation explains the method behind the current breeding program, its progress so far and the challenges involved in managing a breeding program restricted to a captive population with a small founder population.

title: Using community-based data collectors to assess the status of the traditional shark fishery in Madagascar

authors.affiliation: Blue Ventures Conservation/ University of Exeter

abstract_text: Madagascar’s >5,000 km coastal waters harbour an estimated 123 elasmobranch species. Despite the enormous biodiversity and economic and social value of Madagascar’s sharks, the country has no coherent shark conservation strategy. A major barrier to establishing effective, national-scale conservation of sharks is the paucity of information on their ecology, fisheries and socioeconomic value, in particular for isolated fishing communities where dried shark fins are a significant source of income. We monitored shark landings in 19 villages in SW Madagascar between 2007-2012 using community-based data collectors from each village. Community members were trained to collect biological and fisheries data on sharks landed in the traditional fishery (non-motorised vessels), and to use digital cameras to visually record catch to verify species and size. In six years >20,000 shark landings, of more than 25 different species, were documented, of which 20% were classified as immature. Two species, Scalloped Hammerhead Sphyrna lewini and Sliteye Shark Loxodon macrorhinus, accounted for 66.5% of landings. Community focus groups suggested the decline in numbers recorded since 2009 was due to a reduction in shark fishing in this region, with migrant fishers moving to less exploited shark fishing grounds. Despite the unreliability of national export statistics, it is likely that the fishery in Madagascar’s EEZ is severely underreported. We estimate that up to 40,000 sharks/year are landed in the traditional fishery in the Toliara Province alone. Combined with recent by-catch and illegal fishing estimates of 4300 tonnes/year, there is a clear need for management action across all fishing sectors.

title: “Science & Fishery Collaboration”: a new collaborative approach to scientists and fishermen actively working together to provide evidence and inform policy needs

authors.affiliation: Centre for Environment, Fisheries and Aquaculture Science (CEFAS), UK

abstract_text: Cefas scientific research combines a variety of different approaches in order to collect high resolution temporal, spatial, behavioural and biological data of elasmobranches to meet UK policy need. Such approaches include direct engagement and collaboration with UK commercial fishermen, whose livelihoods are ultimately affected by changes to stock assessments, advice and management of their fisheries. Through Defra and EU funded elasmobranch research programmes, Cefas scientists engage and work in partnership with fishermen who regularly encounter elasmobanch species, rapidly and efficiently collecting valuable ‘real-time’ data, required by stock assessors and policy makers. Key to the success of these programmes is direct engagement with fishermen, utilisation of commercial fishing vessels as ‘scientific platforms’ and direct harnessing of fisher expertise and knowledge. Different approaches will be described highlighting examples of current Cefas research programmes with their suitability for application in two very different commercial fisheries; the South West UK off-shore gill net fishery with a by-catch of Spurdog Squalus acanthias, Porbeagle Lamna nasus, and Common Skate Dipturus batis ‘complex’; and the South East UK inshore mixed fishery with a restricted quota of Thornback Ray Raja clavata, leading to substantial discarding of the species. New collaborative roles expected of the fisherman, the scientist, the advisor and the policy maker in such collaborative approaches will be illustrated, along with the potential benefits, challenges and impact of each approach.

title: Shark hand signals for shark identification

authors.affiliation: Shark Academy, Italy

abstract_text: Hand signals are the common way for scuba divers and swimmers to communicate underwater. Divers use signals for emergency purposes, routine communication and for general reasons such as to indicate a marine life form to the buddy. This communication method has multiple advantages: it is simple, effective and easy to use. Each signal is characterized by a gesture, which immediately identifies the shark in question. It refers to gestures one can make with one or two hands and are completed by the position of the arm. These signals let one not only communicate the type of shark which is coming close, but also to know in which direction to look. As a matter of fact, if a seabed shark is signalled (benthonic) the diver will look among the rocks and not upwards, as instead one would if it referred to a surface shark (pelagic). The information therefore supplies, the position of the shark, and would not only be used in case of danger, but having once checked the shark species, the diver could decide to avoid the wrong type of behaviour, with incorrect movements, inciting the shark to attack, but would also make taking photos and filming easier, as well as confirming the precise identification or a useless encounter in the case of uncertainty. It is important to be able to directly encounter the shark head on if one is trying to identify it and to get out of the water with both the same opinion about the sighting: this lets one be more precise in filling in any identification file. To know the movements of differing shark species and their habitat, gives indirect information about the whole marine ecosystem.

title: Bycatch or targeted fisheries? Artisanal shark fishing in Fiji, South Pacific

authors.affiliation: Program Man-Society-Environment, Dept of Environmental Sciences, University of Basel

abstract_text: Artisanal fisheries comprise more than 95 % of the world’s fishermen. Although the main purpose of artisanal fisheries is supposedly subsistence, in fact excess catch or high value products such as shark fins are increasingly sold to gain additional income. Here, we present a first quantitative description of artisanal shark fishing in Fiji. Our major aim was to explore the extent of targeted and bycatch fisheries. 254 semi-structured interviews were conducted with fishermen from villages and communities associated with the coastline of Viti Levu, Vanua Levu, Taveuni, Ovalau and a number of islands of the Mamanucas and Yasawas. Of 254 fishermen interviewed, 15 % reported to target sharks, and 70 % reported to have sharks as bycatch while only 15 % do not catch sharks at all. Those specifically targeting sharks are mainly interested in selling shark fins, reflecting Fiji’s role as a turntable in international shark fin trade. Of the 70 % having sharks as bycatch, 18 % reported to sell fins. The most commonly captured species were Blacktip Reef Sharks Carcharhinus melanopterus and Whitetip Reef Sharks Triaenodon obesus. To confirm these reports and to account for difficulties in species identification by non-experts, 25 tissue samples collected from fishermen and/or local markets were analyzed using the COI locus. We identified ten coastal shark species and confirmed catch reports of endangered or vulnerable species such as Sphyrna lewini and Nebrius ferrugineus. Additionally, we found several cases of misidentification by fishermen, highlighting the importance of molecular approaches in managing artisanal small-scale fisheries.

title: Basking Shark Watch and wider science and conservation in the NE Atlantic – an update

authors.affiliation: Marine Conservation Society, UK

abstract_text: 25 years of Basking Shark watch sightings have revealed considerable spatio-temporal trends of shark occurrence in the British Isles. Hotspots of shark sightings persist in the Southwest, Isle of Man and western Scotland. The treatment of the data to reduce the impact of observer bias has shown that strong North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) years are persistent with longer Basking Shark surface sightings seasons, and that sea surface temperature (SST) appears to be the key signal of the onset of Basking Shark surface feeding. Other research has suggested that a reduction in surface plankton concentration appears to lead to the tailing off of the Basking Shark sightings. Concomitant conservation work focused around the UK Biodiversity Action Plan for the species has led to the successful annexation of the species on the Bonn Convention of Migratory Species since tagging studies have proven international migrations of the species. Although there has been considerable progress in the conservation and knowledge of essential habitat requirements of the species at different spatial scales, fundamental questions such as population numbers, and population trends are still beyond us. Despite these issues, an international Basking Shark conference on the Isle of Man in 2009 recommended that the database is continued, because of its long-term spatio-temporal time series. It demonstrates that public sightings schemes have considerable worth when combined with rigorous scientific research, and applied conservation work.

title: Diel patterns in vertical movement and locomotor activity of Whale Sharks at Ningaloo Reef

authors.affiliation: Bioscience, College of Science, Swansea University

abstract_text: Activity patterns of animals often relate to environmental variables such as food availability and predation pressure. Technological advances are providing us with new tools to monitor and better understand these activity patterns. We used animal-attached data loggers recording acceleration and depth to compare activity patterns and vertical habitat use of Whale Sharks Rhincodon typus at Ningaloo Reef, Western Australia. Whale Sharks showed a moderate reverse diel vertical migration but exhibited a clear crepuscular pattern in locomotory activity. Peak activity occurred at sunset, whereas vertical movement peaked prior to this. Typical ram surface filter feeding could be identified and occurred primarily during sunset and the first hours of night. At such times, direct observations indicated whale sharks were feeding on tropical krill swarms. Diel patterns in activity and diving suggest that whale sharks have tuned their diving behaviour in anticipation of the formation of these high-density patches which appear to only be periodically, but predictably available at sunset. Our results confirm that diel patterns in vertical habitat selection and vertical movements do not necessarily reflect patterns in activity and foraging behaviour. Direct quantification of activity and behaviour is required in gaining accurate representation of diel activity patterns. We also note that by combining behavioural tracking with environmental monitoring we can start to identify and map regions of seasonal importance, including hotspots for feeding and spawning for example.

title: Structure and dynamics of an unexploited population of the Reef Manta Ray Manta alfredi

authors.affiliation: School of Biomedical Sciences, The University of Queensland, St Lucia QLD 4072, Australia

abstract_text: Reliable abundance assessments are essential to the study of population dynamics and underpin conservation biology and management of a species. Although fishing pressure is a major threat to manta spp., information on the trends and status of many of the species’ subpopulations is lacking. Here we use photographic identification and mark-recapture methods to report on the site affinity, size and structure of an unexploited subpopulation of Manta alfredi in eastern Australian waters. A total of 716 individuals were identified between 2007 and 2012, including 636 at Lady Elliot Island (LEI), southern Great Barrier Reef. Over 60% of individuals were resighted at least once during the study period. Multiple resightings within and among years imply a high degree of site affinity to aggregation sites by individuals. One individual was sighted 11 times at LEI within a 27-year period. The sex ratio of this manta ray subpopulation was significantly biased toward females with an overall 1.3:1 female-to-male ratio. Overall, females were more likely to be resighted than males, however, site visitation at LEI varied between sexes. Robust design population models were used to estimate the population size of the winter aggregation at LEI over a 4-year period. The model estimated up to 532 individuals in the population within one winter season and that survivorship of M. alfredi between consecutive years was exceptionally high (φ~1). Our findings highlighted the importance of aggregation sites for M. alfredi subpopulations, and provide a valuable baseline to assist in the status assessment of exploited manta ray subpopulations.

title: Vertical foraging strategies of Basking Sharks in coastal waters and their implication for population surveys

authors.affiliation: Queens University Belfast / Irish Basking Shark Study Group

abstract_text: The adoption of the distance sampling survey method for estimating Basking Shark density and relative abundance has proven difficult because estimates of time at the surface, under varying conditions, are poorly understood (Sims et al., 2003; Southall et al., 2005; Campana, 2008). Here we explore how variance in vertical prey (zooplankton) distribution under different sea states account for variance in the period of time sharks spend in the top metre of the water column where they are detectable during surveys. Vertical prey distribution was recorded by variable depth sampling (1-30 metres) across a grid of nine coastal sample sites located at Malin Head, Ireland. Zooplankton samples were taken via Von Dorn Bottle and vertical plankton net hauls during calm (Force 0-2) and moderate (Force 3-4) conditions. Shark positions throughout the water column (i.e. depth) were determined at one second intervals using CEFAS G5 Time Depth Recorders (TDR’s) attached for 1-6 days (N=11 sharks). By considering the vertical movements of predators concurrent with estimates of prey field and weather we determined survey weightings applicable to mixed coastal water habitats during calm and moderate conditions.

title: Basking Sharks and oceanic fronts: remotely-sensed ocean front metrics for improving understanding of marine megavertebrate habitat use

authors.affiliation: Plymouth Marine Laboratory, UK

abstract_text: Oceanic fronts delineate between water masses, manifesting as enhanced horizontal gradients in temperature, salinity, density, turbidity or colour. Bio-physical coupling along fronts can drive the formation of pelagic foraging hotspots. Many, taxonomically diverse marine vertebrates are known to associate with fronts, including several pelagic sharks and the giant manta Manta birostris. For example, the planktivorous Basking Shark Cetorhinus maximus is known to exploit rich foraging opportunities afforded by zooplankton aggregation along fronts over a range of spatial scales. Recent advances in remote sensing, coupled with animal tracking/biologging, can now generate high-resolution, individual-level insights into the physical drivers of habitat selection. Composite front mapping enables objective detection of thermal and chlorophyll-a fronts and the derivation of metrics quantifying frontal activity in an animal’s proximal environment. Use of these methods has improved understanding of levels of association between basking sharks and fronts in the North Atlantic. Our findings show strong associations in some cases, with sharks following the surface profile of thermal fronts for several days. Recent collaborative work also identifies persistent open ocean frontal zones as a ‘front line’ in shark conservation, as hotspots of overlap between high-use habitat and intensive pelagic longlining activity. Broad-scale, objective detection of frontal zones and their spatiotemporal dynamics could help in identification of priority conservation areas in the open oceans, where sharks and rays remain largely unprotected from deleterious interactions with anthropogenic activity.
